solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Prize winner, finally official (9)

indicatorNotes.finally: 'finally' points at what comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of 'winner' is used

blocks.note: to prize something is to treasure it; as a noun, a prize is a treasure

annotation.surface: An awards announcement: the prize winner, confirmed at last as official.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prize winner' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'Prize' is TREASURE and 'winner' only lends its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the treasurer is the officer of a club or society who keeps its accounts.

entries.clue: Tortilla stuffed with beans, regularly lacking sauce (7)

indicatorNotes.stuffed with: a stuffed tortilla has a filling put inside it, so the other letters go into TACO
indicatorNotes.regularly lacking: lacking letters at regular intervals: every second letter of 'beans' goes, keeping B, A, S

blocks.note: a taco is a folded filled tortilla
BeAnS with the even letters dropped

annotation.surface: A lunch order: a bean taco, hold the sauce.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface says the taco has no sauce, yet the sauce is the answer: TA(BAS)CO.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tabasco is a brand of hot chilli sauce from Louisiana.

entries.clue: Wide player of little consequence (5)

blocks.note: a cricket term: a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, which gives away a run not scored off the bat
a performer with no lines, a face in a film's crowd scene

annotation.surface: A put-down of a sportsman who plays out wide and does little.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket a wide is one of the extras, runs added to the score that no batsman hit; a film EXTRA is the crowd-scene player.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a wide is a kind of extra in cricket scoring, and an extra is a minor film actor.

entries.clue: A sullen art, playing a comedian (4,6)

indicatorNotes.playing: to play with something is to move it around, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A sulky performance style, as if someone were acting glum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Playing a comedian' looks like an actor taking a role; 'playing' works on the words before it instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Stan Laurel was the thin half of the comedy double act Laurel and Hardy.

entries.clue: Output of a cold, curious, absorbing man (5)

indicatorNotes.absorbing: something absorbing soaks another thing up into itself, so RUM takes HE inside

annotation.surface: A strange man catching a cold and what comes out of his nose.
annotation.walkthrough: RUM as 'odd' is old-fashioned British slang (a rum do). R(HE)UM.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: rheum is the watery discharge from the nose and eyes that a cold produces.

entries.clue: Meat cooked in pan with grouse (5,4)

blocks.note: to pan a show is to roast it, criticise it harshly
grouse and beef both mean complain

annotation.surface: A recipe: meat cooked in a pan with grouse, the game bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pan' and 'grouse' look like a cooking pot and a bird; both are verbs of complaint.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: the dish is a joint of meat cooked in the oven, the traditional British Sunday lunch.

entries.clue: Hybrid Ford put out (5)

blocks.note: a plant or animal bred from two varieties
the verb: to wade over a river at a shallow point

annotation.surface: A hybrid car from Ford, taken off the market.
annotation.walkthrough: A triple definition: 'Ford' looks like the carmaker but is the verb, to cross a river on foot.
annotation.definitionFit: Three senses of one word: a hybrid breed, the act of fording, and the mood of someone put out.

entries.clue: When caught, children surrender (4)

indicatorNotes.When caught: to catch a remark is to hear it, so the word is taken by sound

annotation.surface: Children who give themselves up once they are caught.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' here is heard, not captured, and SEED as children is biblical (Abraham's seed).
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to cede territory or a point is to surrender it.

entries.clue: Elaborate about peeled figs I found (9)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so ORNATE goes round the inserted letters
indicatorNotes.peeled: a peeled fruit has lost its skin, so 'figs' loses its outside letters

blocks.note: fIGs without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Someone describing, at length, some peeled figs they came across.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found' is the verb to set up, not the past of find. OR(IG + I)NATE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to found a movement is to originate it, to bring it into being.

entries.clue: Being overheard is unnerving for leaders (7)

indicatorNotes.Being overheard: what is overheard reaches you by ear, so the words are taken by sound

annotation.surface: Being eavesdropped on is unsettling for people in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: SHEIKHS has two pronunciations; the one needed rhymes with 'makes'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sheikh is an Arab leader, the head of a tribe, family or state.

entries.clue: Save a singer from massacre (3)

indicatorNotes.from: saving someone from a place takes them out of it, so CHER comes out of the longer word

annotation.surface: A plea to rescue a performer from a slaughter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Save' is the definition in its sense 'except', and it also sets up the rescue in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: save and but both mean except, as in all save one, all but one.

entries.clue: Poem by a Northern diner, drunk on beer (11)

indicatorNotes.drunk: someone drunk is all over the place, so the letters of 'diner' are jumbled
indicatorNotes.on: in an across answer, what is on the beer comes after it

blocks.note: by = times, the multiplication sign X, as in 3 by 4

annotation.surface: Verse written by a northern diner who has had too much beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like authorship but is the X of 3 by 4.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: an alexandrine is a twelve-syllable line of verse, the metre of classical French poetry.
annotation.definitionNote: Strictly an alexandrine is a verse line rather than a whole poem.

entries.clue: Tie-wearing British like us, with The Times (10)

indicatorNotes.wearing: a word wearing another has it on, round itself, so B sits inside STALEMATE

blocks.note: a chess stalemate is a tie, a draw

annotation.surface: A British gent in a tie, one of us, reading The Times.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Us' is the newspaper printing the clue: The Sunday Times and The Times share an owner. STA(B)LEMATE.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: stablemates share a stable or owner, as the two Times papers do.

entries.clue: Founder of a little business in Kent (4)

indicatorNotes.a little: only a little of the phrase is used, a short stretch from inside it

annotation.surface: The person who started a small firm in Kent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Founder' looks like a person who starts a business; it is the verb, as a ship founders. Kent is a county in south-east England.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb sense: a ship that founders fills with water and goes down.

entries.clue: Anger badly managed on the whole (2,3,5)

indicatorNotes.badly managed: something badly managed ends up in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A verdict that, overall, someone handles their temper poorly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' does double duty: its letters are fodder and it helps signal the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: by and large means generally, taking everything into account.

entries.clue: Surrey, one-handed, casually making a century (3,7,5)

indicatorNotes.casually: done casually is done without order or care, so the letters are thrown together

annotation.surface: A Surrey cricketer batting one-handed and casually scoring a hundred.
annotation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county with a cricket team, and in cricket a century is a hundred runs; here it is a span of time.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition of time: a century is a period of a hundred years.

entries.clue: Vehicle, say, in dash from the South (6,3)

indicatorNotes.in: STATE is placed in the other word
indicatorNotes.from the South: a down answer normally reads from the north; from the south it reads upwards, reversed

blocks.note: to dash is to race; reversed to ECAR

annotation.surface: A car making a dash north from the south of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is the verb, state. E(STATE)CAR.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an estate car, a station wagon in American English, is a type of vehicle.

entries.clue: Feeling uneasy, one visits Dr Psycho anyhow (9)

indicatorNotes.visits: a visitor goes into a place, so I joins the doctor's letters
indicatorNotes.anyhow: done anyhow is done carelessly, in no order, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A patient, anxious, going to see a scary-sounding doctor anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has a nervous patient; 'Dr Psycho' is simply the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dysphoric means in a state of unease or dissatisfaction, the opposite of euphoric.

entries.clue: What could make nettin’ and post to frame goals (7,2,6)

blocks.note: the six letters of a word meaning purpose rearrange to spell NETTIN
post = mail, written to frame, set out, what you aim to do

annotation.surface: Football talk: what the netting and posts that frame the goals are made of.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: the letters of the word INTENT could make NETTIN. The goals and posts are not football at all.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal document: a letter of intent sets out in writing what a party means to do.

entries.clue: Part of the ear heard noise unrefined (7)

indicatorNotes.heard: what is heard is taken by sound, so the two words are said aloud together

blocks.note: a row is a din, rhyming with cow

annotation.surface: Some part of someone's ear picked up a crude noise.
annotation.walkthrough: Say LOBE ROW quickly and it is LOW BROW: the B slides from the first word to the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lowbrow means lacking intellectual or cultural refinement.

entries.clue: Opening rejected by play’s author (7)

indicatorNotes.rejected: something rejected is sent back, so SLOT is turned round
indicatorNotes.by: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: a slot is an opening; reversed to TOLS

annotation.surface: A playwright turning down an opening night.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Play's author' looks like one phrase, a dramatist; the apostrophe-s is 'is', linking wordplay to 'author'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Leo Tolstoy was the Russian author of War and Peace.

entries.clue: Wife worried about large insect (4)

indicatorNotes.about: to turn about is to face the other way, so ATE is reversed

blocks.note: as in 'what's eating you?': ate = worried; reversed to ETA

annotation.surface: A wife fretting about a big bug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but turns ATE round.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the weta is a giant cricket-like insect of New Zealand, among the heaviest in the world.

entries.clue: Maximum measure of digital protection? (10)

blocks.note: the surface wants computer security; the setter means a guard for a digit, a finger, when sewing
as much as that guard can hold when filled to the brim

annotation.surface: A question about the most security a computer system can have.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Digital protection' sounds like cybersecurity; it is a thimble on a finger, and a THIMBLEFUL is a tiny amount.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: the most a thimble can hold is a thimbleful, so the grand 'maximum' is in fact a very small quantity.

entries.clue: Something fruity produced by male. Musk? (5)

annotation.surface: A man's fragrance with a fruity note, perhaps a musk scent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Musk' looks like a perfume ingredient but is Elon Musk. There is also a musk melon.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the melon is a large, sweet, juicy fruit, so 'something fruity' covers it.

entries.clue: Frequency with which a philosopher brought up a goddess (5)

indicatorNotes.brought up: brought up means raised, so in a down answer the name is read upwards

blocks.note: A. J. Ayer, the British philosopher; reversed to REYA

annotation.surface: How often a philosopher raised the subject of a goddess.
annotation.walkthrough: A. J. Ayer was a 20th-century British philosopher, a crossword regular.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Freya is the Norse goddess of love and fertility.

entries.clue: Vessels blowing bass hooters? (4)

indicatorNotes.blowing: to blow a chance or money is to lose it, so BOWLS loses its B

annotation.surface: Ships sounding deep horns, their foghorns booming.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hooters' looks like horns; it is birds that hoot.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful coinage: the birds are named by their call, the hoot, so they are the hooters of the night.

entries.clue: Silly brawl with old biker about Aussie singer (11)

indicatorNotes.Silly: something silly is senseless and out of order, so the letters of 'brawl' are jumbled
indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so ROCKER goes round the anagram

blocks.note: rockers were 1960s British bikers, rivals of the mods

annotation.surface: A pointless fight between an ageing biker and an Australian pop star.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aussie singer' sounds like a pop star but is a bird. ROCK(WARBL)ER.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the rock warbler is a small songbird found only in New South Wales, Australia.

entries.clue: One’s seen in ponds, close to the banks in fact (3)

indicatorNotes.close to: the close of something is its end, so the last letter of 'the' is taken
indicatorNotes.banks: a river's banks are its two edges, so only the outside letters of 'fact' are kept

annotation.surface: A pond creature seen near the banks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to the banks' reads as 'near the shore'; it splits into 'close to the' and 'banks in fact'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an eft is a newt, especially a young one, and newts live in ponds.

entries.clue: Weapon’s initial thrust forward produces angry talk (5)

indicatorNotes.initial thrust forward: a thrust pushes something ahead, so the first letter is shoved on to the far end

blocks.note: a sword is a weapon; its S moves to the end

annotation.surface: A swordsman's first lunge sparks a row.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thrust' belongs to swordplay in the surface; in the wordplay it just pushes a letter along.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to have words with someone is to argue with them.

entries.clue: Extremely noteworthy cryptic with a recent anniversary (9)

indicatorNotes.Extremely: take the extremes, the two ends, of 'noteworthy'
indicatorNotes.cryptic: something cryptic is puzzling and obscure, so the letters are disguised by rearranging

annotation.surface: A remarkable crossword marking a recent anniversary.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue celebrates its own crossword series reaching a hundred years; 'cryptic' looks like the puzzle but is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind: a centenary is the hundredth anniversary of an event.
